title: Thermochemistry
note: Heat flowing into a system is positive, heat leaving is negative. At constant pressure the heat of a reaction equals its enthalpy change, ΔH; exothermic reactions have ΔH < 0. Enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH values add (Hess's law): reverse a reaction and ΔH changes sign, double it and ΔH doubles. q = mcΔT gives heat from a temperature change.

read.title: Following the heat
text: Thermochemistry divides the world into the system, the chemicals you care about, and the surroundings, everything else. When a reaction releases heat, the system loses energy and the surroundings warm up: the reaction is exothermic and its enthalpy change, ΔH, is negative. A cold pack works the other way. Dissolving ammonium nitrate absorbs heat from your skin, so ΔH is positive and the process is endothermic.

Heat is measured through temperature changes. The equation q = mcΔT says the heat equals the mass times the specific heat times the change in temperature. Water has an unusually high specific heat, 4.184 J/(g·°C), which is why it is the standard liquid in calorimeters and why lakes change temperature slowly.

Because enthalpy is a state function, ΔH depends only on where a reaction starts and ends, not on the route. This is Hess's law. If you know ΔH for two steps, you can add them to get ΔH for the overall change, reversing a step changes its sign, and scaling a step scales its ΔH. Tables of standard enthalpies of formation make this systematic: subtract the total for the reactants from the total for the products. Elements in their standard states are set to zero, which gives every table a common baseline.
